corrected_value.title: Producing meaningful improvements in problem behavior of children with autism via synthesized analyses and treatments

decisions.quote:
Abstract Recent literature has described the analysis
and treatment of problem behavior that involves an
open-ended interview to inform the conditions under
which problem behavior is likely to occur, conducting
a synthesized contingency analysis, and implementing
treatment that includes functional communication train-
ing, delay and denial tolerance training, and increasing
the amount of demands presented after a denial (e.g.,
Hanley et al. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis,
47(1), 16–36, 2014). This process has been described
as an Interview-Informed Synthesized Contingency
Analysis (IISCA) or practical functional assessment.
Much of the literature evaluating the practical functional
assessment has originated from authors within the same
research group. The purpose of the present study was to
replicate and extend previous research on the practical
functional assessment with a different group of re-
searchers and in a different setting (i.e., an early inten-
sive behavioral intervention clinic).
decisions.location: Abstract (lines 39-57); see also Introduction (lines 118-146) and References (lines 1264-1268)
decisions.reason: Shipped row 124 identifies Hanley et al. (2014) (DOI 10.1002/jaba.106), which is the sole study cited in the Abstract to define the practical functional assessment (IISCA) and multi-component treatment from the original research group that the present study's stated purpose was to replicate and extend with an independent research group in an EIBI clinical setting. Addressing the blind coder's objection that Strand and Eldevik (2018) is the closest study in a replication chain while Hanley et al. (2014) only introduces background/materials: first, the 20-question interview instrument came from Hanley (2012), whereas Hanley et al. (2014) is the primary empirical study establishing the synthesized contingency analysis and full treatment sequence (FCT, delay and denial tolerance training, compliance chaining, and parent extension) in a clinical setting (lines 118-136); second, the authors frame their study as parallel to Strand and Eldevik (2018) ('the second successful replication of the practical functional assessment and IISCA-informed treatment within a different research lab', lines 1219-1222, replicating 'the practical functional assessment and treatment described previously in several studies by a limited number of researchers', lines 1061-1065), rather than only re-testing Strand and Eldevik (2018) (which was already adjudicated separately as missing_row target_index 0).

decisions.quote:
This study demonstrated the successful replication of
the practical functional assessment and treatment de-
scribed previously in several studies by a limited num-
ber of researchers within an early intensive behavior
intervention (EIBI) program in a clinical setting. Fol-
lowing the contingency analysis and treatment, de-
creases in the frequency of problem behavior and in-
creases in the frequency of desirable behavior were
observed.
decisions.location: Discussion (lines 1061-1069); see also Abstract (lines 61-64) and Discussion (lines 1219-1222)
decisions.reason: Following Codebook Step 3 Rule 1, the authors state an explicit overall verdict that this study demonstrated a 'successful replication of the practical functional assessment and treatment described previously in several studies by a limited number of researchers' (i.e., Hanley et al. 2014 and colleagues) and that 'The results were similar to previous research with an overall reduction in problem behavior and increases in functional communicative responses and compliance with demands' (lines 61-64). Noted clinical and design limitations (single participant, ongoing precursor body tensing, session count, and unmeasured treatment integrity) do not retract the authors' explicit overall verdict of successful replication.

decisions.quote:
Although this is a promising line of research,
much of the literature evaluating the interview informed
synthesized contingency analysis (IISCA) or practical
functional assessment has originated from researchers
within the same group and occurred within a university
outpatient clinical setting, which families would visit 3 to
4 days per week for 1 h of treatment (e.g., Hanley et al.
2014). To date, only one other research group has pub-
lished a successful replication of an IISCA and treatment
in a home-based setting within an early intensive behav-
ior intervention program (Strand and Eldevik 2018).
However, given the perceived drastic change in the ap-
proach to problem behavior, replication across multiple
sites and researchers is still warranted. Therefore, the
purpose of the present study was to replicate and extend
previous research on the practical functional assessment
with a different group of researchers in a different setting
(i.e., an early intensive behavioral intervention clinic).
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding agree on record_type='replication'. The authors collected new primary behavioral data with a new participant (an 8-year-old child with ASD in an EIBI clinic) to re-test the practical functional assessment (IISCA) and multi-component treatment reported by Hanley et al. (2014).
